messages.author: 83b63066408210ec
messages.subject: Different results depending on whether I apply a function in the transformed parameters or model
parts:
So I'm fitting a model that goes like this:

data {
    int <lower = 1> time;
    
    int <lower = 0> successes [time];
    int <lower = 0> total [time];
}

parameters {
    real <lower = 0, upper = 1> initial
    real <lower = 0, upper = 1> asymptote;
    real <lower = 0> scale;
}

transformed parameters {
    real theta_logit [time];
    for (i in 1:time) {
        theta_logit = logit (asymptote + (initial - asymptote) / (1 + (i - 1) / scale));
    }
}

model {
    initial ~ beta (1, 1);
    asymptote ~ beta (1, 1);
    scale ~ gamma (1, 1);
    for (t in 1:time) {
        if (total [t] > 0) {
            successes [t] ~ binomial_logit (total [t], theta_logit [t]);
        }
    }
}


It does not converge, and the results are all wrong. However, if I move the "logit" function from the transformed parameters section to the model section:

data {
    int <lower = 1> time;
    
    int <lower = 0> successes [time];
    int <lower = 0> total [time];
}

parameters {
    real <lower = 0, upper = 1> initial
    real <lower = 0, upper = 1> asymptote;
    real <lower = 0> scale;
}

transformed parameters {
    real theta_logit [time];
    for (i in 1:time) {
        theta_logit = asymptote + (initial - asymptote) / (1 + (i - 1) / scale);
    }
}

model {
    initial ~ beta (1, 1);
    asymptote ~ beta (1, 1);
    scale ~ gamma (1, 1);
    for (t in 1:time) {
        if (total [t] > 0) {
            successes [t] ~ binomial_logit (total [t], logit (theta_logit [t]));
        }
    }
}


Then that converges and works wonderfully.

What's up with that?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Different results depending on whether I apply a function in the transformed parameters or model
parts:
Not the same model. In one case, you only compute logit (theta_logit [t])
when total[t] > 0. So I'd guess logit's getting passed an illegal value (NaN
or outside of (0, 1)) and it's throwing an exception, which halts an iteration.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Different results depending on whether I apply a function in the transformed parameters or model
parts:
If you are sure total[t] is always going to be greater than zero,
put a lower bound of 1 in the declaration and remove the test in the model
block and make sure you still get the same answer.

But I'm still going to stick with my guess that one of your transformed
parameters is NaN.

I'd suggest instrumenting the code with prints to make sure the argument
to logit is in (0, 1) exclusive (perhaps inside conditionals that test if the argument
is out of range if n is large).

- Bob

No reason those models should return the same results.

You can get bad values when you take

Okay so it turns out that when all total values are strictly positive it does converge nicely but when they're zero it doesn't, so you're probably right about that. Is there a way to deal with that case with transformed parameters or should I just put it in the model?

messages.author: 83b63066408210ec
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Different results depending on whether I apply a function in the transformed parameters or model
parts: Well, the scale's already constrained to be positive, but I'm wondering how to deal with the case where the "total" datum of a binomial likelihood is zero. Unless the binomial lpdf Stan function already takes care of that?

On Wed, 22 Feb 2017 at 14:10 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
Always put actual constraints on your data in the model (not
interval priors because you think the value should be in the
interval, but hard constraints like scales being positive).

- Bob

> On Feb 22, 2017, at 10:03 AM, Pedro Carvalho <pedro...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Okay so it turns out that when all total values are strictly positive it does converge nicely but when they're zero it doesn't, so you're probably right about that. However, no iterations seem to halt, or if they do they don't tell me this, they merely say that there were some divergent transitions. Is there a way to deal with that case with transformed parameters or should I just put it in the model?
>
> (Incidentally, putting the transformation in the model actually made it run faster.)
>
> On Fri, 17 Feb 2017 at 18:52 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> If you are sure total[t] is always going to be greater than zero,
> put a lower bound of 1 in the declaration and remove the test in the model
> block and make sure you still get the same answer.
>
> But I'm still going to stick with my guess that one of your transformed
> parameters is NaN.
>
> I'd suggest instrumenting the code with prints to make sure the argument
> to logit is in (0, 1) exclusive (perhaps inside conditionals that test if the argument
> is out of range if n is large).
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
>
> > On Feb 17, 2017, at 3:34 PM, Pedro Carvalho <pedro...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > That's a thing that could possibly happen, yeah, but in the data I actually have no illegal value is ever passed, total [t] is always greater than 0 and the iterations never halt, they just don't converge.
>
> No reason those models should return the same results.
>
> >
>
>
> You can get bad values when you take
>
> > asymptote + (initial - asymptote) / (1 + (i - 1) / scale)
>
>
> and scale is unconstrained.
>
> >
> > On Fri, 17 Feb 2017 at 18:32 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > Not the same model.  In one case, you only compute logit (theta_logit [t])
> > when total[t] > 0.  So I'd guess logit's getting passed an illegal value (NaN
> > or outside of (0, 1)) and it's throwing an exception, which halts an iteration.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Feb 17, 2017, at 2:48 PM, Pedro Carvalho <pedro...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > So I'm fitting a model that goes like this:
> > >
> > > data {
> > >     int <lower = 1> time;
> > >
> > >     int <lower = 0> successes [time];
> > >     int <lower = 0> total [time];
> > > }
> > >
> > > parameters {
> > >     real <lower = 0, upper = 1> initial
> > >     real <lower = 0, upper = 1> asymptote;
> > >     real <lower = 0> scale;
> > > }
> > >
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >     real theta_logit [time];
> > >     for (i in 1:time) {
> > >         theta_logit = logit (asymptote + (initial - asymptote) / (1 + (i - 1) / scale));
> > >     }
> > > }
> > >
> > > model {
> > >     initial ~ beta (1, 1);
> > >     asymptote ~ beta (1, 1);
> > >     scale ~ gamma (1, 1);
> > >     for (t in 1:time) {
> > >         if (total [t] > 0) {
> > >             successes [t] ~ binomial_logit (total [t], theta_logit [t]);
> > >         }
> > >     }
> > > }
> > >
> > >
> > > It does not converge, and the results are all wrong. However, if I move the "logit" function from the transformed parameters section to the model section:
> > >
> > > data {
> > >     int <lower = 1> time;
> > >
> > >     int <lower = 0> successes [time];
> > >     int <lower = 0> total [time];
> > > }
> > >
> > > parameters {
> > >     real <lower = 0, upper = 1> initial
> > >     real <lower = 0, upper = 1> asymptote;
> > >     real <lower = 0> scale;
> > > }
> > >
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >     real theta_logit [time];
> > >     for (i in 1:time) {
> > >         theta_logit = asymptote + (initial - asymptote) / (1 + (i - 1) / scale);
> > >     }
> > > }
> > >
> > > model {
> > >     initial ~ beta (1, 1);
> > >     asymptote ~ beta (1, 1);
> > >     scale ~ gamma (1, 1);
> > >     for (t in 1:time) {
> > >         if (total [t] > 0) {
> > >             successes [t] ~ binomial_logit (total [t], logit (theta_logit [t]));
> > >         }
> > >     }
> > > }
> > >
> > >
> > > Then that converges and works wonderfully.
> > >
> > > What's up with that?
> > >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Different results depending on whether I apply a function in the transformed parameters or model
parts:
You mean y ~ binomial(N, theta) where N == 0?
I'm pretty sure that will require y to be zero to not
throw an exception, and if that's the case, it should return
0 (== log 1). If it doesn't do that, either just remove
the y = 0, N = 0 cases from the data set or put a conditional
in a loop to evaluate them. They can't add any information about
theta obviously.

- Bob
